newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian coal industry at the crossroads.
newsitem.headline: Australian coal industry at the crossroads.

text.p: Australia's coal industry - the nation's biggest export earner - is facing a battle for survival as mining companies hit by high costs, low prices and plummeting productivity, begin to buckle under global competitive pressures.

Poor coal price settlements by Australian producers with Japan for 1997/98, exacerbated by struggles with coal mining unions over enterprise agreements, have led to some companies looking to quit the industry altogether.
"With the prospects we have in 1997, if we don't do anything different ... profitability will disappear," the chairman of the New South Wales Minerals Council, Terry O'Reilly, told Reuters.

O'Reilly, also managing director of leading semi-soft coking coal producer, Coal and Allied Industries Ltd, said lower cost structures together with higher productivity were vital for the survival of Australian coal companies.

Poor returns and union difficulties have fuelled market speculation that RTZ-CRA may sell out of its Hunter Valley coal operations in New South Wales, involving the sale of its 71 percent of Coal and Allied.

U.S.giant Atlantic Richfield Co has already gone, putting its Arco Coal assets in Queensland's Bowen Basin up for sale this month while Exxon Corp has its New South Wales coal mining assets up for auction to the highest bidder.
RTZ-CRA has described an impending exit from its New South Wales coal operations as "pure speculation."

Chief executive Leon Davis said in a speech to U.S. analysts that the Coal and Allied mines were higher cost operations. "RTZ-CRA believes that strong Asian demand, broad micro-economic reforms and improved industrial relations augur well for its current and potential Australian coal operations," he said.
Analysts said RTZ-CRA, together with its counterparts in the Queensland coal industry, have been at the forefront of attempts to streamline industrial relations.
"Coal workers are paid well but no longer is there public support for the old unionism," said Maree Klemm, analyst with Brisbane broker Morgan Stockbroking Ltd.

Klemm said economies of scale were now being sought by coal companies in an industry where pay levels of up to A$150,000 a year for some surface workers and up to A$100,000 a year for miners were common. "It is going to be a make-or-break year for (coal industry) industrial relations," she said.

A Melbourne coal analyst agreed, stating costs, not prices, were the only consideration for companies in the coal industry. Attempts by producers to introduce enterprise agreements with coal mining unions were only the first stage of an impending struggle between owners and workers, the analyst said.

Enterprise labour agreements are based on individual operations rather than the industry as a whole. "This year will be particularly tough. It would appear we are heading into uncharted industrial relations waters," the analyst said.
The exit of some industry players is despite a bullish coal production outlook from Queensland, the country's biggest coal-producing state.

"By the year 2000, Queensland coal production is expected to grow to 150 million tonnes annually, resulting in a dramatic increase in export value over the A$4.2 billion in 1995/96 (to June 30)," Queensland Department of Mines and Energy director-general Bob Day has said.
This increase from the current 93.7 million tonnes means new players could be attracted to Queensland, analysts said.
"This could see the return of the South Africans as well as purchases of further assets by local companies including BHP, QCT Resources and Shell International," one analyst said.
